module_title: Union Executive - Discretionary Powers, Vetoes, and Amendments
introduction: This advanced level analyzes the President's Veto powers, the binding nature of the Council of Ministers' advice (42nd & 44th Amendments), and the Prime Minister's role as the pivot of the Cabinet system.

core_concepts.title: Presidential Veto Powers (Article 111)
core_concepts.description: 1. Absolute Veto: Withholding assent. 2. Suspensive Veto: Returning for reconsideration (overridden by simple majority). 3. Pocket Veto: Taking no action. (India has no Qualified Veto like the USA).

core_concepts.title: Constitutional Amendments (42nd & 44th)
core_concepts.description: The 42nd Amendment (1976) made the advice of the Council of Ministers binding on the President. The 44th Amendment (1978) added that the President can return advice ONCE for reconsideration, but the reconsidered advice is binding.

core_concepts.title: Situational Discretion of the President
core_concepts.description: Unlike the Governor, the President has no 'constitutional' discretion, only 'situational' discretion: 1. Appointment of PM when no party has a majority. 2. Dismissal of CoM if it loses confidence. 3. Dissolution of Lok Sabha if CoM loses majority.

core_concepts.title: Relationship between President and PM (Article 78)
core_concepts.description: It is the duty of the PM: 1. To communicate all decisions of CoM to the President. 2. To furnish information regarding administration as the President may call for.

important_entities.name: Kitchen Cabinet
important_entities.significance: An informal circle of 2-4 influential colleagues/friends whom the PM consults on important matters; not mentioned in the Constitution.

important_entities.name: Article 143 (Advisory Jurisdiction)
important_entities.significance: The President can seek the opinion of the Supreme Court on questions of law/fact. The SC's opinion is not binding on the President.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: The President has NO veto power over Constitutional Amendment Bills. After the 24th Amendment (1971), it is obligatory for the President to give his assent to such bills.
The President cannot use a Suspensive Veto for Money Bills. He must either give assent or withhold it.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: A simple way to remember that for Constitutional Amendment Bills, the President cannot say no or return them.

exam_strategy_tips: Focus on the 'Basic Structure' doctrine regarding how much Parliament can limit the President's situational discretion.
Understand the distinction between 'Aiding and Advising' (Art 74) and the PM's duty to inform (Art 78).
